header:
Date: 2025-11-05 | Start: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 72m
Attendees: Jordan Mills (Redwood AE), Priya Khatri (Redwood SE), Liam Ortiz (Redwood Eng Ops); Alex Romero (Helix CTO), Mina Patel (Helix Infra Lead), Samir Rao (Helix Security), Eve Chen (Helix ML)
summary: Technical deep-dive focused on air-gapped delivery of a sealed inference bundle, offline license activation, GPU driver compatibility, and runtime performance tradeoffs. Discussed bundle packaging (PGP-signed tarball vs signed ISO), checksum/manifest verification, secure courier vs SFTP over controlled jumpbox, driver/kernel constraints for CUDA/cuDNN, KV cache warmup strategies for on-prem workloads, batching and latency SLOs, and quantization/precision tradeoffs for cost vs throughput. Agreed next steps for runbook, manifest delivery, and a dry-run activation date.
topics: runtime perf: KV cache, batching, latency/throughput
quantization strategy and impact on hallucination risk
transcript:
[00:00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hi everyone, thanks for carving out the time. We thought we'd run through the sealed bundle flow and the GPU compatibility checklist so the onsite team can do a dry-run with minimal internet.
[00:00:23] Alex (Helix CTO): Hey thanks, yeah we need to be airlocked for regulatory reasons, so anything that needs external calls has to have an offline mode or a fallback.
[00:00:39] Priya (Redwood SE): Yep, we'll show the bundle handshake, the signed manifest, and the offline license activation token flow. Quick note: in the bundle we include a driver matrix, signed checksum (sha256), and an adaptive runtime with both quantized and full-fp kernels.
[00:01:05] Mina (Infra): On drivers—our infra currently runs RHEL 8.7 kernel 4.18 variant patched; we have a mix of A100 40GB and RTX A5000 nodes. What exact driver versions are required?
[00:01:28] Priya (Redwood SE): For the A100s the recommended driver is the NVIDIA 525+ branch and CUDA 11.8, but we also have runtime fallbacks compatible with 515-ish if you can't upgrade immediately. For A5000s, 515+ generally works. We will include a compatibility matrix in the manifest. Note: kernel module parameters like nvidia-drm modeset can affect mmap/IPC perf.
[00:01:55] Samir (Security): Can you walk through how the license gets activated without the hosts contacting Redwood's control plane?
[00:02:12] Jordan (Redwood AE): Sure — offline activation is a signed license blob. We sign the license with our HSM-backed key; you bring the blob onto the air-gapped cluster and run the offline activation script which verifies signature locally. The bundle is PGP-signed as well.
[00:02:39] Eve (ML Eng): Is there any telemetry that requires outbound? If we disable telemetry, do we still get model regression alerts?
[00:02:52] Priya (Redwood SE): In fully air-gapped mode telemetry is disabled. You can optionally run a periodic export job that packages anonymized evals and we can ingest them via secure physical transfer, but automatic regression alerts need connectivity.
[00:03:12] Alex (CTO): Hmm ok. We prefer manual export for regulatory chain.
[00:03:27] Priya: Noted. About the bundle transfer methods: two options — secure courier with encrypted SSD (we provide manifest + PGP signature), or a controlled jumpbox scp over a one-time-only ephemeral VPN tunnel. Courier is simpler from a security perspective but slower.
[00:03:53] Mina: For us courier is acceptable but we need chain-of-custody logs and tamper-evident seals. Can we have the manifest include hardware serials and a packing list?
[00:04:09] Jordan: Yes, we'll include a packing manifest, checksum file, and a human-readable chain-of-custody checklist.
[00:04:25] Priya: Moving on to runtime: we saw in your trial workload that prefix repetition is high, so KV cache warmup will be important. For on-prem we support two cache modes — persistent KV on disk-backed store for long-term reuse, and in-memory prewarm at boot. The persistent option needs a stable disk backing with fsync guarantees.
[00:04:52] Samir: What is the tradeoff in latency when roaming from in-memory KV to disk-backed?
[00:05:06] Priya: Disk-backed cold hits can be 3–8x slower on the first accesses, so for latency SLOs under 100ms we recommend in-memory warmup plus periodic checkpointing. We also ship a prewarm tool in the bundle that can replay saved prefixes to warm caches.
[00:05:31] Eve: That prewarm tool — does it generate real tokens that would affect billing logic if we were metered?
[00:05:44] Jordan: In Dedicated/Private contracts we don't meter by token in the same way; the prewarm runs are marked as maintenance mode and are excluded from usage reporting in the signed manifest.
[00:05:59] Mina: On batching — we need guidance for 95th percentile latency under 200ms for our interactive product vs throughput for nightly batch jobs.
[00:06:15] Priya: Configurable routing policies handle that. You can pin latency-critical routes to low-batch-size pools (batch size 1–4) and route background jobs to high-batch pools (batch size 16–64). The runtime supports continuous batching with dynamic thresholds; it can cap batch latency. There's also an adaptive policy that drops into smaller batches when queue latency budgets approach SLO.
[00:06:49] Alex: What about quantization? We saw Q4_0 and Q8_0 options in the docs — what's the expected perf delta and quality hit?
[00:07:02] Priya: Q4-style quantization (4-bit) gives 2–3x memory reduction and about 1.5–2.5x throughput increase depending on kernel support, but can introduce subtle hallucination shifts for some instruction-heavy prompts. Q8 gives less compression but more fidelity. We recommend running a small eval suite from your prompts; we include example eval harnesses in the bundle.
[00:07:28] Eve: Any recommended quantization-for-accuracy technique — mixed-precision layers or per-channel?
[00:07:37] Priya: We use per-channel asymmetric quant when possible and keep attention/softmax in higher precision; we also ship a hybrid kernel where embedding and LM head stay fp16. The manifest will include suggested layer freeze lists.
[00:07:54] [00:08:10] Liam (Redwood Eng Ops): Quick interjection — for drivers we found that the NVML backwards compatibility sometimes trips with older dcgm collectors; bundle includes a vetted DCGM build. If you use vendor-supplied exporters, run them in a sidecar container with the pinned libc.
[00:08:35] Mina: Good to know — our monitoring team runs Prometheus exporters from the node image.
[00:08:46] Priya: On offline licensing specifics: the offline license blob is time-bound and single-instance for the sealed bundle. For renewals we will generate a new signed blob and exchange via the same courier chain. We also support a hardware-bound license keyed to the system UUID if you want device-tied activation.
[00:09:09] Samir: For hardware binding, what prevents someone cloning the VM image?
[00:09:17] Priya: We check hardware UUIDs and optionally require TPM-backed attestation. The runbook has TPM-based activation steps; if you don't have TPM, we can fall back to MAC and UUID checks plus manual approval.
[00:09:37] Alex: Can you summarize the verification steps our ops should run once the SSD arrives?
[00:09:45] Jordan: Sure — (1) verify physical seals and chain-of-custody form, (2) compute sha256 of the sealed ISO and compare to manifest PGP-signed file, (3) verify PGP signature with Jordan's public key (we'll share), (4) mount the bundle in a containment namespace, run checksum on each file, (5) run driver install scripts in dry-run mode, (6) run activation: offline-activate --blob /path/to/blob --verify-only, check exit code and logs.
[00:10:23] Mina: If a host fails driver install due to kernel mismatch, do you provide a rolling compatibility image or we must upgrade kernel?
[00:10:35] Priya: We include both prebuilt driver binaries and the build scripts to compile against your kernel. In constrained networks it's often easier to install the signed binary; otherwise run the provided dkms flow. We'll add notes for RHEL 8.7 specifics in the runbook.
[00:10:52] Eve: Runtime perf testing — can Redwood provide a synthetic runner that mimics our 95th percentile prompt mix?
[00:11:03] Priya: Yes, we include a perf harness with configurable workload profiles (prompt lengths, prefix reuse, batch sizes). We'll also share sample config files and a small dataset to mimic your production prompt patterns.
[00:11:22] [00:11:40] Jordan: A couple of gotchas we've seen: (1) SELinux in enforcing mode can block the runtime mmap of shared kv segments — we include a policy module but recommend a scoped SELinux policy, (2) some enterprise images strip out user namespaces which breaks container nonroot helpers, (3) kernel preemption settings affect soft real-time performance.
[00:12:06] Samir: We'll have to coordinate with our sec team; they prefer minimal new selinux policies, so maybe a conservative approach.
[00:12:18] Priya: Understood — we can include an audit-only policy and a suggested minimal exception list in the runbook.
[00:12:30] Alex: About model rollouts — can we do a canary on a subset of nodes offline?
[00:12:38] Priya: Yes, the runtime supports version pinning per-route. The canary flow in air-gapped mode is manual: deploy the model artifact to the canary nodes, flip the route configuration locally, collect local metrics, then roll. The console in private deploy will be available on your control plane instance (not us) if you choose the Private control plane option.
[00:13:02] Mina: Any storage recommendations for persistent KV?
[00:13:09] Priya: Use NVMe-backed volumes with wear-leveling and disable aggressive GC; ext4 or xfs with barriers enabled. Provide at least 2x expected KV size for headroom. We also support sharded KV across nodes for larger workloads.
[00:13:30] Eve: Does the bundle include model quantized variants or do we quantize post-delivery?
[00:13:39] Priya: We can ship both: baseline fp16 and optional quantized builds (Q4, Q8). In some regulated environments customers prefer to run quantization in-house; in that case we provide the quantization toolchain with fixed seeds and scripts.
[00:13:58] Jordan: Quick interlude — Alex asked earlier about fallbacks if a driver isn't supported. If a GPU driver is incompatible we can fallback to CPU slow path for critical routes, but throughput will be severely impacted. We recommend testing the fallback in the dry-run.
[00:14:21] Alex: Ok. Also, what about interactions with our existing license server for OS packages? Can Redwood's activation integrate with our internal CA?
[00:14:33] Priya: We can sign license blobs with an intermediate cert that you verify against your internal CA; the runbook has a section to exchange public certs and enable CA verification at activation.
[00:14:50] Mina: Regarding the prewarm — how long to warm a 40GB A100 KV for our typical 60k token prefix set?
[00:14:59] Priya: Prewarm time depends on disk IO and parallelism; on NVMe with parallel jobs you can see warm times in the 10–30 minute range for that scale. The prewarm tool has concurrency knobs.
[00:15:19] Samir: Any particular kernel flags we should check to optimize NVMe throughput?
[00:15:27] Liam: Ensure I/O scheduler is mq-deadline or none, disable swap, set readahead appropriately. We'll add exact sysctl recommendations in the runbook.
[00:15:41] Alex: On security docs — are you able to send SOC2 and your private deployment whitepaper?
[00:15:49] Jordan: Yes we'll attach SOC 2 Type II and the on-prem security whitepaper. For air-gapped specifics we'll include a dedicated appendix.
[00:16:05] [00:16:30] Priya: A few last operational notes: (1) the bundle includes a small diagnostics binary that runs health checks and uploads a zipped log when reconnected, (2) we sign each model shard manifest and include shard hashes so you can verify integrity post-transfer, (3) the driver installer runs with --dry-run to report missing kernel headers first.
[00:16:56] Eve: Great. Can we get an example of the manifest format?
[00:17:02] Jordan: We'll send a template — it's a YAML manifest with keys: name, version, sha256, driver_matrix[], kernel_min, certs[], and chain_of_custody[]. We'll PGP-sign that manifest.
[00:17:18] Mina: One operational edge-case — we're using central image builds that strip debug symbols; does the runtime need those?
[00:17:27] Priya: Not required for normal operation, but the debug symbols help root-cause perf regressions. We'll include stripped debug packages optionally.
[00:17:40] Alex: Ok let's recap and lock dates.
[00:17:45] Jordan: Recap: Priya will produce an airlocked runbook + driver matrix by 2025-11-10; Jordan will send PGP key + manifest template by 2025-11-07; Helix to confirm node inventory and kernel versions by 2025-11-12; plan a dry-run activation week of 2025-11-24. Any objections?
[00:18:06] Alex: Sounds good.
[00:18:12] Samir: We'll also send our internal chain-of-custody process doc.
[00:18:19] Jordan: Perfect — thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and a calendar invite for the dry-run.
[00:18:28] [End of recording — truncated transcript for brevity; full call ~72 minutes]
